Mechanism of Intracellular Accumulations

Inadequate removal and degradation of an endogenous substance

Excessive production

Deposition of abnormal exogenous material

Fatty Change (Steatosis)

Abnormal accumulation of triglycerides within cells

Most often seen in the liver but also could occur in the heart, skeletal muscle, kidney and other organs

Mostly caused by alcohol abuse and diabetes

Cholesterol & Cholesteryl Esters

Cellular cholesterol metabolism is highly regulated

Phagocytic cells may become overloaded with lipids in pathologic conditions characterized by increased intake or decreased catabolism of lipids (e.g., atherosclerosis)

Proteins

Less common than lipid accumulations

In nephrotic syndrome, excessive amounts of resorbed albumin accumulate in vesicles in the tubular epithelial cells seen as pink, hyaline cytoplasmic droplets

Marked accumulation of immunoglobulins in the rough ER of some plasma cells forming rounded, eosinophilic Russell bodies

Glycogen

Associated with abnormalities in the metabolism of either glucose or glycogen

Examples: Diabetes & Glycogen storage diseases

Pigments

Pigments are colored substances that could be endogenous or exogenous

Carbon

Lipofuscin

Melanin

Hemosiderin

Carbon

Most common accumulated exogenous pigment (air pollutant)

When inhaled, it is phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages and transported to lymphatic channels to the regional lymph nodes

Lipofuscin

Insoluble brownish- yellow granular intracellular pigment

Accumulates in heart, liver, and brain

Occur with aging (wear and tear pigment)

Melanin

Brown-black pigment that is synthesized by melanocytes

Acts as a screen against harmful ultraviolet radiation

Hemosiderin

Yellow to brown granular pigment derived from hemoglobin

Accumulates in tissues where there is a local or systemic excess of iron

Hemosiderin accumulations are usually pathologic except small amounts in bone marrow, spleen and liver phagocytes
